phonemes.desc: Stressed first syllable [alt], with the voiceless lateral cluster typical of Arrernte orthography; the lateral 'l' is followed by a palatalised release into 'tj'.
High front vowel [i] preceded by the lamino-palatal affricate 'tj' [c], a sound common in Central Australian languages.
Final syllable [ɾə], with a tapped 'r' and a reduced vowel in unstressed position.

pronunciation.approximation: 'AHLT-chi-ruh' — stress the first syllable, pronounce the 'tj' as the 'ch' in 'church', and let the final syllable relax.

pronunciation.note: The name is Arrernte, not Greek or Sanskrit, so it has no 'original script' in the classical sense. The ASCII form altjira flattens the distinctive palatal cluster and removes the capital that marks a proper name; the restoration Altjira is the scholarly citation form.

domains.title: The Eternal Sky Being
domains.subtitle: The Dreaming, Creation, and the Sky Above
domains.lead: Altjira is the eternal sky being of the Arrernte peoples of Central Australia. In the early ethnographic record he is described as the uncreated creator: he made the earth, shaped its first features, and then withdrew to dwell forever in the sky. His feet are said to be like those of an emu, and he never needs to bend, because the sky is high and he is eternal. Behind the figure lies the deeper Arrernte concept of altjira — the Dreaming — the timeless ground of law, country, and ancestral identity.

cards.name: The Eternal Sky
cards.desc: Altjira dwells in the sky above, unborn and undying, the source from which the visible world was shaped.

cards.name: The Dreaming
cards.desc: Altjira names the timeless epoch in which ancestral beings travelled, made country, and left law for the living.

cards.name: Creation of the Earth
cards.desc: He formed the land, its waterholes and ranges, and then ascended to the sky, leaving the world for his children.

cards.name: Ancestral Law
cards.desc: The stories and ceremonies that bind people to country are carried as sacred trust by Arrernte custodians.

symbols.name: The sky
symbols.meaning: The eternal canopy where Altjira dwells and from which creation descended.

symbols.name: Emu footprints
symbols.meaning: His feet are likened to those of an emu, a sign of his other-than-human nature and his connection to the Australian land.

symbols.name: The Milky Way
symbols.meaning: In Arrernte cosmology the sky river is camp and road for ancestral beings, linking earth and heaven.

symbols.name: Waterholes and ranges
symbols.meaning: Features of country created during the Dreaming and maintained through ceremony today.

mythology.lead: The mythology of Altjira comes to us through Arrernte oral tradition and the early ethnographies of Spencer and Gillen, Carl Strehlow, and later scholars. The stories are not entertainment; they are title deeds to country, instructions for ceremony, and maps of moral responsibility. Some details are held by initiated custodians and are not shared in public space.

myths.title: The Uncreated Creator
myths.text: In the account recorded by Spencer and Gillen, Altjira is eternal: he was not born and will not die. In the beginning he made the earth and all that it contains — its hills, waterholes, plants, and animals — and then he rose into the sky, where he remains with his two sons. The earth was left for the ancestors who followed and for the human beings who would inherit their law.

myths.title: The Sky Above
myths.text: Altjira lives in the sky, high above the camps of men and women. His feet are like the feet of the emu, and he never bends them, because the sky is wide and there is no obstacle in his path. The stars and the Milky Way are the camps and tracks of ancestral beings, so that the night sky is read as a mirror of the country below.

myths.title: Alcheringa
myths.text: The term alcheringa — rendered from Arrernte altjira — names the Dreaming: the time when the ancestors moved across the land, creating its forms and leaving behind the songs, designs, and ceremonies that maintain it. Altjira is both the name of the eternal sky being and the name of the epoch in which the world received its present shape. Later Arrernte scholarship, especially T. G. H. Strehlow, stressed that altjira primarily means 'to dream' and refers to the eternal creative order rather than to a single personal deity.

myths.title: Custodianship
myths.text: The public, scholarly record of Altjira is only one layer of knowledge. Arrernte custodians hold song-cycles, designs, and ceremonial responsibilities that are not published and are transmitted under strict traditional protocols. PuniCodex presents only the documented, open scholarly account and acknowledges that deeper knowledge belongs to the communities who keep it.

etymology.derivation: The name comes from Arrernte altjira, meaning 'to dream' or 'the Dreaming', the timeless creative order underlying the world. In early missionary and ethnographic literature the term was rendered as Alchera or Alcheringa and was sometimes personified as a supreme sky being. The word thus carries both a specific mythological usage and the broader cosmological sense of Aboriginal law and identity.

originalScriptNote: Arrernte is an oral language with no indigenous writing system historically attested for individual names. The form Altjira is a modern scholarly romanisation of an Arrernte word. It should therefore be labelled 'Scholarly Transliteration' rather than 'Original Script'. The ASCII form altjira is a DNS compromise; the capitalised restoration Altjira is the conventional citation form.
syncretism: Altjira entered Western scholarly discourse chiefly through the ethnographies of Spencer and Gillen and the Lutheran missionary Carl Strehlow. Early accounts tended to present Altjira as a 'high god' or creator, an interpretation that later Arrernte custodians and scholars have revised. T. G. H. Strehlow argued that altjira is better understood as the Dreaming itself — the eternal, sacred order — and not as an anthropomorphic deity comparable to the God of biblical monotheism. In popular and esoteric literature the term 'Alcheringa' has been borrowed widely, sometimes detached from its Arrernte roots. PuniCodex follows the scholarly consensus that respects both the early record and the later corrections offered by Arrernte tradition-bearers.
culturalLegacy: The word Alcheringa — the Dreaming — has become one of the most widely recognised Aboriginal English terms in the world. It names not only a cosmology but a legal, artistic, and environmental framework that continues to shape Aboriginal identity in Central Australia and beyond. The concept influenced Australian art movements, land-rights discourse, and interfaith dialogue. Altjira also appears as the name of an Aboriginal art centre (Altjira Aboriginal Art) and in creative works that draw on Arrernte themes. Its importance lies less in personal cult than in the enduring idea that the land is a living record of sacred law.
extendedMeditation:
Altjira asks us to think about time differently. The Dreaming is not a long-ago past; it is the continuing ground of the present. The ancestors did their work, but the work is not finished — it is renewed every time a song is sung, a design is painted, or a custodian walks country.

To meditate on Altjira is to meditate on the relationship between sky and land, eternity and responsibility. The sky being withdraws but does not abandon; he leaves the world in the care of those who come after. That is the moral heart of the Dreaming: the land is a gift and a trust, and those who hold it are answerable to the ancestors and to the future.
